title: Primary financial markets are where new securities and assets are sold by borrowers and sellers to investors
claim: Financial markets enable borrowers to find lenders and equity owners to locate investors. Primary markets are where new securities and assets are sold by governments, companies, and hard asset producers. Secondary markets exist where investors trade with each other.
support: Foundational concept for understanding market structure
mechanism: Primary/secondary market distinction enables price discovery and capital formation
assumptions: Price discovery occurs through competitive mechanics
validation: Fundamental market structure concept, widely validated in finance literature

title: Debt vs Equity as fundamental investment choices
claim: Financial markets offer two basic investment choices: debt (lending to governments or companies) or equity (buying shares or ownership stakes). Debt represents a promise to pay with required interest payments and repayment on a schedule. Equity means full or partial ownership.
mechanism: Debt instruments have scheduled cash flows; equity has residual claims and unlimited upside
assumptions: Equity holders benefit from business growth

title: Three Rs framework: returns, risks, and relative value
claim: Financial markets analysis rests on three fundamental Rs: (1) returns, comprising interest on bonds and dividends on stocks; (2) risks that reduce those returns; (3) relative value, determining whether an asset is cheap, expensive, or fairly valued.
support: Core analytical framework for asset evaluation
mechanism: Returns drive cash flows; risks discount expected value; relative value determines entry/exit points
assumptions: Assets are valued based on risk-adjusted expected cash flows
validation: Aligns with modern portfolio theory and fundamental analysis

title: Three analytical approaches to investment decisions: fundamental, technical, and quantitative analysis
claim: Three basic types of analysis guide whether to go long or short: (1) fundamental analysis examines prospects using top-down (macro) or bottom-up (micro) approaches; (2) technical analysis studies prices and patterns to predict future moves; (3) quantitative analysis uses mathematical formulas on collected data to guide decisions.
mechanism: Each approach encodes different information signals and assumptions about market efficiency
assumptions: Price history contains information about future returns
validation: Standard taxonomy in financial literature; widely practiced

title: Long and short positions: definition and return mechanics
claim: Investors with a long position own a security or hard asset and profit when the price increases. A short position is established by selling a borrowed security; the holder gains when the price drops.
support: Foundational definition of directional exposure mechanics
mechanism: Long position has unlimited upside, limited downside (loss of principal); short position has unlimited loss potential, limited upside (sale price minus cost)

title: Governments issue bills (<=1 year), notes (<=10 years), and bonds (>10 years) to finance budget deficits
claim: Governments compete with companies to raise money in financial markets. They issue bills (IOUs paying off within a year), notes (maturing up to 10 years), and bonds (for longer periods) to bridge gaps between spending and tax revenue. The size of the budget deficit determines borrowing need.
support: Foundational framework for fixed income markets
mechanism: Government debt maturity structure reflects borrowing needs and interest rate risk distribution

title: Currency markets reflect returns on bank deposits and government security holdings
claim: When deciding where to invest cash, investors effectively make currency and interest rate choices. Holding cash in a bank account or keeping it at home involves implicit currency positioning and exposure to interest rates offered by depository institutions.
support: Links currency exposure to fixed income decisions
mechanism: Cash management involves dual choice: currency and rate; foreign cash implies forex risk

title: Companies raise short-term funds through money market instruments similar to government bills
claim: Companies compete with governments to raise money in financial markets. Like governments, they can raise funds for one year or less by selling securities similar to government bills. For longer financing periods, they use notes and bonds.
support: Corporate short-term funding structure parallel to government markets
mechanism: Money market instruments offer flexibility and lower cost for short-term borrowing
assumptions: Companies have access to capital markets
Credit markets price company risk correctly

title: Equity (partial ownership) is a unique financing source unavailable to governments
claim: Companies have a financing option unavailable to governments: selling partial ownership, or equity. This allows investors to distinguish between companies and purchase shares in different enterprises.
support: Distinguishes corporate from sovereign financing; enables equity pricing
mechanism: Equity has no maturity, residual claim, and voting rights

title: Hard assets (gold, commodities, real estate) are tangible alternatives to financial securities
claim: Hard assets are alternatives to stocks, bonds, and cash with a physical presence beyond computer records. Gold is favored by many investors as a separate asset class. Commodities and real estate are other hard asset examples.
mechanism: Physical store of value; limited supply; inflation hedge properties
validation: Standard portfolio theory includes alternative assets

title: Indexes track market performance and enable performance assessment and passive investment
claim: Indexes enable investors to track how well or poorly financial markets are performing. They provide ways to assess individual investor performance or that of hired managers. Index-based funds allow investors to invest in the overall market.
support: Indexes as dual-purpose tools: benchmarks and investable vehicles
mechanism: Index construction aggregates individual securities; enables systematic portfolio construction and benchmark tracking
assumptions: Index methodology is transparent and consistent
Passive investing can match market returns

title: Derivatives: value tied to underlying securities or rates
claim: Derivatives are contracts whose value is tied to some other investment, such as a stock, bond, interest rate, currency, or index. Basic types include futures, options, and swaps.
mechanism: Leverage through contingent contracts; enables hedging, speculation, and tactical positioning

title: Futures and forwards are derivative contracts for future delivery or settlement
claim: Futures and forwards are contracts where the value is determined by the underlying asset (stock, bond, rate, currency, or index) at a future date. They obligate the buyer and seller to transact at a predetermined price.
support: Defines forward market mechanics and price determination
mechanism: Forward price reflects spot price, interest rates, carry costs, and time to maturity; futures add daily settlement and standardization
assumptions: No default risk in standardized futures

title: Options provide asymmetric payoff profiles with limited downside for buyers
claim: Options and warrants are contracts granting the right (not obligation) to buy or sell an underlying asset at a predetermined price. Call options give the right to buy; put options grant the right to sell. The buyer's risk is limited to the premium paid.
support: Defines option asymmetry and leverage characteristics
mechanism: Option premium reflects probability of exercise and volatility; leverage enables small capital deployment for large exposure
assumptions: Options are priced by Black-Scholes or similar models
validation: Standard options mechanics and pricing theory

title: Swaps allow exchange of cash flows between counterparties
claim: Swaps are contracts allowing two parties to exchange cash flows. Interest-rate swaps exchange fixed and floating payments. Credit default swaps provide insurance against default.
support: Defines swap mechanics and primary use cases
mechanism: Swaps enable interest rate hedging, credit risk management, and structured positioning without ownership transfer
assumptions: Cash flow streams are known or predictable
validation: Standard derivatives instruments; heavily regulated post-2008

title: Mutual funds and ETFs pool investor capital with professional management
claim: Mutual funds and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) aggregate capital from many investors. Fund value is based on investments selected by a manager. Alternative funds for wealthier investors offer more complexity and higher costs.
support: Defines fund structures and value proposition
mechanism: Pooled capital enables diversification, professional management, and economies of scale
assumptions: Managers add value through stock selection
Fund fees are reasonable relative to performance
validation: Standard fund structure; widely empirically studied
